strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: group-robust classification under spurious correlations without bias annotations at training or validation time.

The proposed BEO idea is simple and intuitively appealing: using overfitting and iterative high-confidence subset selection to recover pseudo-bias groups. The method is lightweight and easy to integrate with existing group-aware methods such as GroupDRO and DFR.
The empirical scope is reasonably broad, covering Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments, cMNIST, and cCIFAR10, with comparisons to supervised, validation-supervised, and fully bias-agnostic baselines.
The results on multi-class synthetic benchmarks are strong, especially relative to CCDB, suggesting that finer-grained pseudo-group reweighting can be useful in highly biased settings.
The ablations separating BEO from FG-CCDB are helpful and show that pseudo-bias labels can recover a substantial fraction of the benefit of human bias annotations in some settings.
weaknesses: The technical formulation of FG-CCDB appears problematic. If group weights are intended to align each class-conditional distribution with the marginal distribution, Equation 3 gives W_ij = q_i / P_ij, but Equation 4 then divides by N_ij for the per-sample weight. Under standard weighted sampling, the resulting group mass is proportional to W_ij rather than W_ij * P_ij = q_i, so the claimed exact distribution matching does not follow. This undermines a central theoretical claim of the method.

The method relies on a strong structural assumption |Y| = |S| and assumes each class is spuriously correlated with a single abstract bias attribute. This excludes many realistic settings with multiple simultaneous bias attributes, non-class-aligned biases, continuous biases, or asymmetric group structures. The paper acknowledges some limitation but does not adequately evaluate or solve it.

The main gains on real-world binary datasets are mixed. On Waterbirds the improvement over CCDB is negligible, on CelebA iid accuracy drops substantially, and on CivilComments the method is better but the paper does not deeply analyze why several annotation-free methods exceed fully supervised baselines. The strongest improvements are mostly on synthetic multi-class benchmarks.

Some baselines appear potentially under-tuned or not fully comparable, especially the surprisingly weak supervised GroupDRO results on cMNIST/cCIFAR10 relative to bias-agnostic methods. The paper would benefit from clearer hyperparameter parity, model-selection details, and stronger recent baselines for multi-class group robustness.

The model selection protocol is somewhat unclear. The paper claims no bias annotations during validation, but selects the best model by worst-class validation accuracy. This is plausible, but it is not consistently distinguished from worst-group selection, and the implications for imbalanced or multi-class settings need more careful discussion.

The evaluation of bias discovery focuses on aggregate group prediction accuracy but does not provide enough quantitative detail in the extracted tables about per-group precision/recall, confusion matrices, or failure modes. Since BEO is central, more rigorous analysis of when pseudo-bias labels are wrong is needed.

The paper is closely built on CCDB and overfitting-based bias discovery, so the novelty is incremental rather than transformative. The contribution is useful, but the conceptual ingredients are largely recombinations of known ideas.

Reproducibility is only moderate: implementation details are partially provided, but code availability, exact preprocessing, baseline tuning, and validation protocols are not sufficiently specified. The manuscript also contains many grammatical and typographical errors that reduce clarity.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and active problem: group robustness under spurious correlations without access to bias annotations during training or validation.
The method is simple and potentially practical: it combines overfitting-based pseudo-group discovery with closed-form group reweighting, avoiding expensive per-sample feature storage used by CCDB.
The empirical section covers several standard benchmarks, including Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments, cMNIST, and cCIFAR10, and reports averages over multiple seeds.
The ablations attempt to separate the contribution of the bias exploration module from the proposed reweighting module.
weaknesses: There appears to be a serious technical issue in the core reweighting derivation. Eq. 3 defines a group multiplier W so that W[:,j] * P[:,j] = q, but Eq. 4 then converts this to a per-sample weight by dividing by N_ij. If samples in group (i,j) are weighted by W_ij / N_ij, the resulting weighted class-conditional group mass is not proportional to W_ij P_ij and generally will not equal q. This undermines the claimed exact distribution matching and the mutual-information argument at the center of FG-CCDB.

The novelty is limited. Bias exploration through overfitting/high-confidence or misclassified examples is closely related to JTT, LfF, SELF, XRM, and bias amplification methods. The paper does not clearly establish why the proposed BEO procedure is a conceptually new contribution rather than a simple variant of existing overfitting-based pseudo-group discovery.

The method relies on restrictive assumptions that are not adequately handled: |Y| = |S|, each class is dominated by a single abstract bias attribute, and the bias predictor's output space aligns with bias labels. These assumptions are known to fail in realistic settings with multiple spurious factors, non-class-aligned attributes, or asymmetric group structure; the paper itself notes failures for CelebA/CivilComments-like patterns but does not resolve them.

The evaluation does not convincingly support the broad claims. On real-world datasets, gains over CCDB are small on Waterbirds, mixed on CelebA, and stronger mainly on CivilComments; several comparisons to supervised baselines are not clearly favorable. The strongest improvements are on synthetic cMNIST/cCIFAR10 setups that match the paper's assumptions unusually well.

Validation/model selection is unclear and potentially inconsistent with the stated no-bias-annotations setting. The appendix says the best model is selected by highest worst-class validation accuracy, while the main comparisons emphasize worst-group robustness. It is not clear how this criterion is chosen, how it compares fairly to baselines using group validation labels, or whether hyperparameters/repetition counts were tuned using group information.

The ablation in Table 3 weakens some claims: BEO-substituted GroupDRO/DFR often remain noticeably below their supervised counterparts, and FG-CCDB with human annotations only marginally improves over unsupervised FG-CCDB in some cases. This does not strongly establish BEO as a substitute for annotations or FG-CCDB as superior to standard group balancing.

The paper lacks robustness analyses that are important for this problem: sensitivity to the 10% split, top-50% confidence threshold, number of BEO repetitions, group-count errors, class imbalance, multiple simultaneous biases, and cases where the majority group is not diagonal/class-aligned.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important implementation details are missing or underspecified, no code availability is indicated, and several reported standard deviations are implausibly tiny in Table 3, raising concerns about whether all randomness and model-selection variability are properly accounted for.

Presentation quality is below the standard expected for a top-tier venue, with many grammatical errors, typos, inconsistent naming such as BEO/BOE, and unclear exposition around the mathematical formulation. These issues make it harder to assess the method and its claims.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: group-robust classification under spurious correlations without access to bias annotations during training or validation.
weaknesses: The method relies on a strong structural assumption that the number of latent bias states matches the number of classes and that each class is dominated by a corresponding bias attribute. This is central to BEO and limits applicability to more realistic settings with multiple, hierarchical, continuous, or non-class-aligned biases.

strengths: The paper targets an important and active problem: group-robust learning under spurious correlations without bias annotations.
The proposed MST plus FG-CCDB pipeline is simple, computationally lightweight, and empirically compares against a broad set of supervised, validation-supervised, and annotation-free baselines.
The evaluation covers several commonly used spurious-correlation benchmarks, including Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments, synthetic multi-class settings, and UrbanCars for multiple shortcuts.
The paper includes useful ablations on MST quality, hyperparameters, use of human bias annotations, and integration of MST with GroupDRO/DFR.
weaknesses: The technical contribution is incremental relative to CCDB and existing bias-amplification or failure-based debiasing methods. MST is essentially iterative high-confidence filtering to train a biased model, and FG-CCDB is a closed-form confusion-cell reweighting scheme; the novelty over prior pseudo-group discovery and group reweighting is not fully compelling.

There is a potential soundness issue in the weighting derivation. Eq. 3 gives a mode-level correction for matching conditional bias distributions, but Eq. 4 divides by the mode count and the implementation uses a global WeightedRandomSampler. It is unclear that this actually realizes the claimed class-conditional distribution matching objective, and the paper does not rigorously justify the normalization.

The method assumes the discovered bias label space has the same cardinality as the class label space. This is restrictive and underexplained, especially for multi-shortcut or non-class-aligned biases where the number of bias states may differ from the number of classes.

The central assumption that an overfitted ERM model reliably captures harmful bias cues is only empirically motivated and fails in some settings acknowledged by the authors. The paper does not characterize when MST will identify shortcuts versus noise, label artifacts, class difficulty, or core-feature failures.

The empirical gains are mixed on the main real-world binary benchmarks: improvements over CCDB are very small on Waterbirds, moderate on CivilComments, and larger on CelebA, while i.i.d. accuracy sometimes drops. The strongest gains are on synthetic or highly controlled settings, limiting confidence in broad impact.

The multi-shortcut evidence is not fully convincing. UrbanCars results show favorable gaps, but the comparison is incomplete for several baselines, DDB has much better gap metrics but lower ID accuracy, and the paper does not clearly analyze whether the learned two-class bias proxy captures all shortcut combinations.

Model selection and validation details weaken the label-free claim. The paper selects by worst-class validation accuracy, and many hyperparameter analyses rely on ground-truth mode quality; it is not clear how practitioners without group annotations should choose repetition count, beta, or gamma in less canonical datasets.

Presentation quality is below the expected standard: the PDF appears to include reviewer-response-style sections such as R1W1/R2W2 in the appendix, contains formatting artifacts, cramped tables, grammar issues, and even a stray 'Code:' marker. This substantially hurts professionalism and clarity.

Reproducibility is incomplete: no code or implementation details beyond high-level hyperparameters are provided, several baseline numbers appear copied from prior work with uneven reporting, and some tables omit standard deviations or complete metrics for competing methods.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: group-robust learning under spurious correlations without bias annotations.
The proposed pipeline is simple and computationally plausible: use overfitted auxiliary models to infer bias-like modes, then perform mode-level reweighting.
The empirical section covers several standard benchmarks, including Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments, cMNIST/cCIFAR10, and UrbanCars, and reports multiple seeds for the main proposed method.
The ablations separating MST from FG-CCDB and the analysis of inferred mode quality are useful and show that the authors attempted to diagnose the source of gains.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. MST is largely a variant of existing bias-amplification / train-twice / hard-sample identification ideas, and FG-CCDB is an incremental discretized extension of CCDB using predicted confusion cells. The paper does not clearly establish a sufficiently new conceptual contribution over CCDB, JTT, XRM, uLA, and related bias-amplification methods.

The central theoretical framing is weak. The method claims to minimize mutual information between bias cues and labels, but the actual procedure uses hard predicted labels from an overfitted classifier as a discrete proxy for latent bias features. The connection between this proxy, the true bias variable, and the original CCDB objective is asserted rather than rigorously justified.

The weighting formula is fragile and under-specified. Entries with very small or zero predicted mode counts can produce unstable or undefined weights, yet the paper does not discuss smoothing, clipping, numerical handling, or robustness to mode-prediction errors in a principled way.

The empirical comparison is not fully convincing. Many baselines appear to be taken from heterogeneous sources with different validation assumptions, tuning budgets, and reporting conventions; several entries lack standard deviations. This makes the claimed superiority over recent methods difficult to trust.

The paper’s bias-agnostic claim is somewhat overstated. Model selection uses validation worst-class accuracy, and the method relies on dataset-specific hyperparameters and assumptions about bias-aligned samples being high-confidence and majority within class. The sensitivity analysis itself shows that beta=70% can be better on several datasets, undermining the fixed beta=50% justification.

The method’s scope is narrower than claimed. It depends on ERM overfitting to the harmful shortcut and may fail when shortcuts are not easier than core features, when multiple spurious factors do not align with classifier predictions, or when minority groups are not cleanly represented by confusion-matrix cells.

The multi-shortcut evaluation is thin. UrbanCars is useful, but one dataset is insufficient to support broad claims about multi-shortcut or complex hidden-bias scenarios, especially when the mode definition collapses potentially multiple independent shortcut attributes into a single predicted class index.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence. For example, statements that MST can substitute for human bias annotations or that it is unlikely to miss harmful bias cues are not supported by the experiments or theory.

Presentation quality is poor for a top-tier submission. The manuscript contains many grammatical errors, formatting issues, crowded tables, and appendix text that appears to include response-to-reviewer material, which hurts clarity and professionalism.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper gives high-level optimization settings but lacks enough detail on baseline implementations, tuning ranges, code availability, precise model-selection protocol for all methods, and handling of edge cases in the weighting procedure.

strengths: Addresses an important and timely problem: group-robust learning under spurious correlations without access to bias annotations.

The proposed MST idea is intuitive and useful: exploiting overfitting and high-confidence sample selection to produce pseudo bias partitions is simple, practical, and well motivated by prior observations.

FG-CCDB is a lightweight extension of CCDB that replaces sample-level Gaussian distribution matching with mode-level reweighting, reducing storage and computational overhead while improving empirical performance.
Empirical coverage is strong: the paper evaluates on Waterbirds, CelebA, CivilComments, UrbanCars, cMNIST, and cCIFAR10, including binary, multi-class, and multi-shortcut settings.
Results are competitive and often strong, especially relative to fully bias-agnostic baselines; gains over CCDB on CivilComments and synthetic multi-class benchmarks are particularly convincing.

The paper includes useful ablations and diagnostics: MST quality against ground-truth groups, repetition analysis, hyperparameter studies for gamma and beta, supervised FG-CCDB variants, and runtime estimates.
weaknesses: The theoretical and mathematical formulation of FG-CCDB is not fully convincing. In particular, the transition from mode-level matching weights W_{i,j}=q_i/P_{i,j} to per-sample weights w_{i,j}=W_{i,j}/M_{i,j} is unclear and may not actually preserve the claimed exact class-conditional matching after normalization.

The method relies on a strong structural assumption that the learned bias label shares the same label space as the target class and can be represented by the hard confusion matrix. This is elegant but restrictive, and the paper does not fully characterize when this abstraction fails, especially for multiple independent shortcuts or continuous/attribute-rich biases.

The multi-shortcut evidence is promising but limited. UrbanCars is a useful benchmark, but for binary classification the C x C mode structure has only four modes while the underlying shortcut combinations are richer; more analysis is needed to show that MST can reliably disentangle or cover complex shortcut structures beyond this setting.

Some comparisons are hard to interpret because baselines differ in architecture, validation requirements, reported metrics, and whether numbers are reproduced or copied from prior work. A clearer controlled comparison against the strongest recent label-free methods would strengthen the claims.

The claim that the method matches or surpasses bias-supervised approaches is somewhat overstated. Performance is mixed across datasets, and on Waterbirds the fully supervised DFR/GroupDRO numbers remain stronger than FG-CCDB; the paper should frame the result as competitive rather than broadly superior.

Model selection still uses validation worst-class accuracy. This is less demanding than using group labels, but it is not a fully annotation-free deployment criterion in settings where robust validation labels or balanced validation data are unavailable.

The paper would benefit from code release details and clearer reproducibility information. Hyperparameters are listed, but implementation choices such as handling zero or tiny modes, normalization of weights, and sampler behavior are important for reproducing the method.
Writing quality is generally understandable but has several grammatical issues, notation inconsistencies, and occasional overclaims that reduce polish for a top-tier submission.
